messages.subject: Detection adjustment prior to GLM of count data?
messages.subject_clean: Detection adjustment prior to GLM of count data?
messages.body_plain:
Dear All

Two questions, one practical the other more general. Both probably
demonstrate my inexperience with DISTANCE, in which case I apologise in
advance!

The first question:

I am interested in modelling bird count data (either from point or line
transects) using GLM (e.g. log-linear models with Poisson error term) to
assess the influence of various factors, covariates and their
interactions on the count. In the analysis I would like to take into
account differences in the detection probability (primarily arising from
habitat differences).

It strikes me I can use DISTANCE to calculate probabilities of detection
(by habitat if the sample size allows) and then adjust the raw data for
each count by this figure and then use this adjusted figure in the GLM.
However, if I do this the resulting adjusted density value for the
individual sample will not reflect the variation in the probability of
detection?

In answer to a similar question to this list: "Beyond z-tests" (Maddox,
6 Mar 2002). It seemed (to me!) to be suggested that a weighing vector
could be include to reflect the variation in the detection probability
between habitats and this included in the GLM (presumably with the same
weighting vector value used for all counts in a particular habitat?). Is
this appropriate? What method could I use to identify whether the
detection function in fact varies between habitats (comparing AICs of
various runs pooling the data differently by habitats until I get the
lowest values?).

In answers to this question: "Adjusting counts for detectability and
covariates" (Tucker, 11 May 2004). Another way was suggested, I quote:

"I think you want to fit the detection function using all your data, but
with
habitat as a covariate (which you have done), but then *predict* the
probability
of detection at each point, given the habitat type of the point and that
the
animal is present within the truncation distance.  You then want to
calculate
density (or abundance) at each point using this habitat-specific
probability of
detection.
You can do this in the multiple covariate engine of Distance in the
Model
Definition | Estimate tab.  Under "Quantities to estimate and level of
resolution", for the Density and the detection function rows, tick both
the
"Global" and "Sample" columns.  Make sure you have habitat as a
covariate.  For
more about this, see the online help, Chapter 9, Defining MCDS models,
Estimating the detection function at multiple levels.
The output you will get will be density for each point, and p_i for
animals at
each point too.  (You will also get abundance for each point, but
there's a bug
in Distance where the area used to calculate this is currently wrong so
it's
acutally abunance for the whole study area assuming density at that
point
applies to the whole study area -- this bug is fixed in the next version
of
Distance to be released.)"

If the output I get is "density for each point, and p_i for animals at
each point too" then I could use the "p_i" as the weighting vector?? Is
this a better (different?) or more appropriate way?

Second question (sorry, its very basic compared to the first).

I currently work in conservation in Indonesia and I regularly see
DISTANCE used as a simple recipe for calculating absolute densities,
typically using all default values in the programme (against all
advice!), and without any great understanding of what AICs, CVs, CIs etc
actually mean.

Very small sample sizes often lead to very high variation in estimated
density but this is regularly justified by saying that "the 'real' value
must be within the confidence intervals somewhere". What is the simple
answer to this question? I can tell people that a sample size of 10 will
give you little information on density, or that a CV of over 20%
suggests a pretty inaccurate estimate, but by that point most people
already have a figure for density on the print-out and they are happy!
My question: What combination of criteria would lead you to reject a
density estimate outright?

Yours

Nick Brickle
ni...@brickle.com
Bogor, Indonesia.

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,
I am not sure how to handle the following problem during analysing point
count data of Slaty Solitaires.
I ran the analysis with hazard rate cosine and half-normal cosine
adjustments, using the same distance intervals in both. Seeing the Detection
Probability Plot in the results, it looks like the hazard rat model fits
much better than the half-normal model. But AIC is slightly lower and the
GOF-test little better in half-normal adjustment, so the program would
decide for the half-normal model. But the density using the half-normal
model is almost double as high (reaching a ridiculous value) as with the
hazard rate model.

I would appreciate any advice.

Knut Eisermann

messages.subject: Admin: How to unsubscribe and make other changes to list settings

messages.body_plain:
Dear distance-sampling list members,

There has been a spate of people trying to unsubscribe from the list by
posting messages to distance...@jiscmail.ac.uk.  As almost all of you
know, this does not work - instead the message is forwarded to 600 or so
list members.

To leave the list, send an email to:
jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk
with the message:
leave distance-sampling

Do *not* post messages to
distance...@jiscmail.ac.uk
unless you mean them to be sent to all list members.

Alternatively, you can leave the list by browsing to
http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/
and clicking on the "Subscriber's Corner" link.  Note that you can also
change your list membership settings in the Subscriber's Corner -- e.g., you
can temporarily disable your membership while you're away, or choose to
receive messages in a compact "digest" format.

I am appending the list guidelines, which are sent to all members when they
join.  They contain useful information, such as how to leave the list and
guidelines for appropriate messages, so please save them somewhere safe and
read them before posting to the list.

Thanks!

 - Len Thomas

************************************
* DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK *
************************************

PLEASE SAVE THIS MESSAGE FOR FUTURE REFERENCE,
IT CONTAINS VITAL INFORMATION

Welcome to the DISTANCE SAMPLING e-mail discussion list. The purpose of
this list is to promote the sharing of ideas and information among
researchers and practitioners interested in distance sampling techniques
(see below). Suitable topics for postings include:

o Questions about distance sampling survey design and analysis.
o New methodological developments in distance sampling.
o Use of software tools (program DISTANCE and other software).
o News about up-coming meetings, workshops and conferences where
  distance methods will be discussed.
o Jobs in distance sampling fields.

Instructions for subscribing, unsubscribing, posting and getting help
are given in subsequent sections.

Before posting any messages,

** PLEASE READ THE LIST GUIDELINES **

which are given near the end of this file. Very briefly the key points
are:

o Make sure distance-sampling is the appropriate forum for your message.
  If you are unsure ask the list owner first.
o Use informative subject lines.
o If seeking a reply, include your address in the body of your message.
  Offer to compile the replies you recieve and summarize them to
  the list.
o If replying, consider whether to reply to the sender rather than
  the list.
o Send plain text only (no Word or encoded files or other attachments).
o Do not post commercial advertising (however announcements about
  jobs, conferences, non-commercial software, etc are okay).

 ========================================================================
Background
 ========================================================================

Distance sampling is a widely used technique for estimating the abundance
of biological populations. Distance sampling methods include line
transects, point transects (variable circular plots), cue counting,
trapping webs and migration counts. An introduction to the the
methods is given in the following book:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers, D.L,
and Thomas, L. (2001). Introduction to Distance Sampling.  Oxford University
Press, Oxford, UK.

A previous edition of the book is freely available for download on the
internet
at http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

Recent methodological developments and applications are also discussed in
biological journals such as the Journal of Wildlife Management, Ecology,
Biometrics, and the Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Ecological
Statistics.

The standard software for the design and analysis of distance sampling
data is program Distance. Newer versions are fully windows-based with an
intuitive point-and-click interface. The software is freely available for
download from the Distance home page http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

 ========================================================================
Important Email Addresses
 ========================================================================

1. distance...@jiscmail.ac.uk

This is the address of this list. Any messages sent to this address
will be automatically forwarded to all the members of the list.

2. jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk

This is the JISCmail program. You send commands (such as
join distance-sampling) to this address.

3. distance-sam...@jiscmail.ac.uk

This is the address for the list owner who looks after the list
(currently Len Thomas of the University of St Andrews, UK).

If you have a problem with the list, send a message to this address.

For example,
- if you have problems leaving the list
- if you have problems sending a message to the list

4. jiscmail...@jiscmail.ac.uk

This is the JISCmail Helpline.
If you have any questions about or problems with the JISCmail system
use this address.

 ========================================================================
Important World-Wide Web sites
 ========================================================================

1. http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling.html

This is the list home page. Here you will find information about
the list (this file), an archive of all messages to the list over the
past year, and other files that I may post from time to time.

2. http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk

JISCmail home page. From here you can find out more about how to
manage your list membership, and about the other lists run by the
JISCmail server.

 ========================================================================
How to...
 ========================================================================

1. To send a message to everyone on the list, send an email to:
distance...@jiscmail.ac.uk

2. To leave distance-sampling, send an email to:
jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk
with the message:
leave distance-sampling
--

3. To join distance-sampling, send an email to:
jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk
with the message:
join distance-sampling yourfirstname yourlastname
--
Replace the text "yourfirstname" with your first name and the text
"yourlastname" with your last name
(e.g., join distance-sampling Joan Smith)

4. To find out more about what the JISCmail server can do (for example
searching the monthly archive of messages, suspending mail when you're
on holiday, etc):
a) Check out the web pages at http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk especially
http://jiscmail.ac.uk/docs/user-ref-card.html
b) Send an e-mail to:
jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk
with the message:
info
--
You will then received a list of on-line documentation about
JISCmail, and you can use the "get" command to retrieve those
documents which interest you. For example, the message:
get JISCUSER.REFCARD
will get you the user reference card.

 ========================================================================
List Guidelines
 ========================================================================

Please bear in mind that posting a message to distance-sampling is
equivalent to sending several hundred people individual e-mail messages.
The list is intended to facilitate the sharing of ideas and information,
but if there are too many messages then people will become overwhelmed
and leave the list, so defeating its purpose.

To make each posting as informative as possible, please observe the
following guidelines:

1. Make sure distance-sampling is the appropriate forum for your post.
If your message is not specifically about distance sampling methods,
it belongs somewhere else. An excellent list of statistical lists is
maintained by Stuart Young at http://www.stats.gla.ac.uk/allstat/
A comprehensive, if somewhat out-of-date list of ecological lists was
written by Una Smith and is archived in many places including
http://immwww.jr2.ox.ac.uk/bioguide/ If you are unsure whether your
message is appropriate, send it to the list owner (distance-sampling-
req...@jiscmail.ac.uk) and ask him to tell you.

2. Use informative subject lines.
This will enable people to decide whether your message is of interest
to them, so they can choose whether to read it or not. Everyone is
busy, and messages with uninformative subject lines like "Question",
"Test", "Distance sampling", etc., will probably get deleted by many
people without even being read. Try and make your subject lines
concice but informative, e.g., "g(0) for double-platform minke whale
transects", "Design of VCPs for forest bird surveys", "Workshop: Intro
to distance sampling, New Zealand".

3. If you are asking a question, make sure you have done your homework
first.
Sending a message to several hundred people without putting in at least
a days work on the problem yourself first is rude. There is a lot of
information available about distance sampling which should be consulted
before posting a message, for example the book Introduction to Distance
Sampling by Buckland et al. (http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance).
If you have joined the list recently, you should also check the archives
to see that the question has not been discussed already (archives are at
http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling.html).

4. If you are asking a question, consider requesting that replies are sent
to your e-mail address, and offer to summarize the ensuing discussion
to the list.
By encouraging list members who are interested in your question to mail
you directly, a discussion can be initiated that is not constrained
by the need to keep the volume of list e-mail down. If you then post
a summary of this discussion to the list then eveyone will be able to
read the comments in a concise format, and you may well get further
advice from people. This is especially appropriate if you have a
question that you think will be of minority interest.

5. If you want any replies, include your name and e-mail address your
message.
Some e-mail programs don't let people find this information out unless
it is in the body of your message. Having a "signature" that is
appended to the bottom of all messages is a good idea, so long as it is
short.

6. If you are replying, consider whether to reply to the sender rather
than the list.
If you are sure your answer is correct, and it will be of general
interest then by all means post to the list. Otherwise, consider
sending it directly to the person who asked the question and asking
them to summarize the replies they receive to the list.
Double check where your reply is going to. Look in both the To: field
and the cc: fields - if either says distance...@jiscmail.ac.uk
then your reply will go to the list.

7. Send plain text only (no Word or encoded files or other attachments).
Why no attachments? (i) Many of the people on the list will not be
interested in your particular question, so will not want to see the
dataset/screengrab you are posting. This is frustrating for them if
they spent many minutes downloading your message down a telephone line.
(ii) Many members have a limit on the size of their inbox, so sending a
large attachment can crash their mail system, or prevent them from
receiving any other messages. (iii) Many mail reading programs cannot
deal with attachments, and your message shows up on such systems as a
seemingly random series of ASCII text.
If you want to post extra information, such as data files or screen
shots, what should you do? (i) If you have access to a web server, the
easiest thing is to upload the file there and provide the URL (web
address) in your *plain text* message, so that people can download it
if they want. (ii) You can do a similar thing if you have an anonymous
ftp server - include instructions for accessing the file in your message.
(iii) If you have none of there, offer to email the file to anyone who
asks you for it. You will be surprised how few people do! However,
this way, you can be sure that it will reach those who are interested.

8. Do not post commercial advertising.
The list is not a forum for posting unsolicted adverts to people.
Announcements about job vacancies, conferences, workshops and non-
commercial software releases are fine. If there is any doubt, send
the message to the list owner and it will be forwarded to the list if
it is appropriate.

 ========================================================================
Troubleshooting
 ========================================================================

o Never send commands, or requests to join, or admin. queries, to
distance...@jiscmail.ac.uk - your problem will be broadcast to
all members of the list!

o If something goes wrong - perhaps you get two copies of every message -
send a message to distance-sam...@jiscmail.ac.uk

o If your mail address changes, send a message to
distance-sam...@jiscmail.ac.uk

o If mail from distance-sampling to you is regularly rejected for some
reason (perhaps because you have run out of file space or your computer
mail service has been renamed) the list-owner may eventually delete you
from the list.

o If you get no mail, you may have been deleted from the list - see above.
Either send a message to distance-sam...@jiscmail.ac.uk, or
resubscribe

 ========================================================================
Acknowledgements
 ========================================================================

Thanks to David Borchers, Sharon Hedley, Rachel Fewster, Stuart Young and
Tiago Marques for help with the list guidelines.

Please send comments/suggestions to
distance-sam...@jiscmail.ac.uk

 ========================================================================
End of file
 ========================================================================

--

messages.subject: estimating variance of change in density over time
messages.subject_clean: estimating variance of change in density over time
messages.body_plain:
We have density estimates of foxes from point counts in several areas
over four years. We want to estimate uncertainty around the estimates of
change in density between years for each area.  The detection function
for each area was generated from data pooled over the four years.
Therefore, because the annual estimates are not independent, we think we
need to use equation 3.109 in the 2001 book to calculate the variance of
this change in densities.

The issues are: for any given survey period, we carried out repeat
surveys of the points, with variable effort at each point, therefore we
need to use equation 3.79 to calculate var n.  To this by hand will be
laborious given the number of areas and years involved in our survey.
Does Distance output estimates of var n? If we have to do it by hand,
can we simply calculate var n from the variance of the encounter rate,
by multiplying this with the number of points surveyed?

Gavin

messages.subject: Re: Detection adjustment prior to GLM of count data?
messages.subject_clean: Detection adjustment prior to GLM of count data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick, list,

What you're proposing is what we sometimes call "spatial modelling" or
"spatial density surface estimation".  I'll attempt an answer, but I'm no
expert so others may want to contribute more.  Also, there's some stuff on
this in Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.

To begin with, you need to do the detection function modelling in Distance.
You could either stratify by habitat, or put habitat in as a factor
covariate in the MCDS engine.  If you have enough data, and no problems such
as avoidance, rounding, etc, then you could try both and let AIC tell you
which is better.  If using MCDS then you could include other covariates too.
Once you've finished this modelling, you want an estimate of detection
probabilty by point (p_k) (Note, I'm omiting hats from estimates to avoid
cumbersome text notation.  Also, for now, I'm assuming you don't have any
species level covariates such as cluster size).  To do this, you ask for
density by sample, as in my reply to  "Adjusting counts for detectability

and covariates" (Tucker, 11 May 2004).

Now you need to incorporate the estimates of p_k into the spatial model for
the bird counts.  To my knowledge there are three ways to do this:

1. Divide the observed count at each point n_k by the estimated p_k to get
an estimate of abundance at each point N_k.  This abundance is non-integer,
so:
2. you might want to divide N_k by the area of each point (pi*w^2) to get an
estimated density at each point D_k.  Doesn't make much difference really.
Either way, your GLM or GAM will no longer have a Poisson error term as the
response variable is non-integer -- perhaps a Gamma?
3. Retain the n_k as the response variable in a Poisson model, but use
pi*nu_k^2 as an offset, where nu_k is the effective detection radius for
that point.

Personally, I prefer 3 as you get to keep the discrete nature of the counts.
However method 3 doesn't work if you have any species level covariates, such
as sex of bird or cluster size.  In that case, you don't know what the
effective detection radius is when you observe no birds -- but you do know
that the estiamate of density is 0.  If you have species level covariates in
1 or 2 you estimate N_k by the sum of 1/p_i for each bird i detected at the
point.  There is a section of the online manual that says how to calculate
p_i for each animal given the parameter estiamtes of the detection function.

In practice, two problems usually present themselves:

1. Overdispersion.  Often many points have 0 birds seen, so you get data
with lots of zeros and relatively few high counts (or high D_ks if the p_ks
are sometimes small).  Can be hard to model.  Can perhaps investigate the
various zero-inflated models that are out there?

2. Variance estimation.  How does one incorporate the variance due to
estimating the detection function in the final variance estiamte from the
spatial model?  An easy way is a nonparametric bootstrap or jacknife of
points, but you need plenty of points for this.  Various parametric
bootstraps have been proposed - I think there is something on this in
Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.  It may be possible to do
something analytic based on the delta method -- don't know.

So, hope this helps -- as I said others may be able to contribute more.
I'll answer your second question in a separate email.

Cheers,

 - Len

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick, list,

> >Second question (sorry, its very basic compared to the first).

> >I currently work in conservation in Indonesia and I regularly see
> >DISTANCE used as a simple recipe for calculating absolute densities,
> >typically using all default values in the programme (against all
> >advice!), and without any great understanding of what AICs, CVs, CIs etc
> >actually mean.

Argh!  Hopefully you can do your bit in training people to make intellegent
use of the program.  Also, I've found in general that people who have a poor
understanding of the program options also have a poor understanding of how
to design surveys and implement field methods that give reliable results.
Just my prejudice I guess.

> >Very small sample sizes often lead to very high variation in estimated
> >density but this is regularly justified by saying that "the 'real' value
> >must be within the confidence intervals somewhere". What is the simple
> >answer to this question? I can tell people that a sample size of 10 will
> >give you little information on density, or that a CV of over 20%
> >suggests a pretty inaccurate estimate, but by that point most people
> >already have a figure for density on the print-out and they are happy!
> >My question: What combination of criteria would lead you to reject a
> >density estimate outright?

I'm afraid it's not that simple.  Getting a reliable estimate requires more
than just an "adequate" sample size of observations, and the required sample
size depends on factors such as the type of survey (points require more than
lines), and shape of the detection function (wide shoulders require fewer
observations to accurately model).  Also, remember that you also need a
"decent" sample size of lines or points for reliable estimation of the
encounter rate variance.

Here's a very rough checklist for initial assessment of a study:

- were the lines/points laid out according to a randomized survey design?
Ideally there should be 20 or more lines or points - many fewer than that
and I'd doubt the encounter rate variance estiamtes.  If the analysis is
stratified, you'd like 20 lines per stratum if possible.

- is g(0) likely to be 1?

- is animal movement likely to be a problem? (is there evasive movement, or
do animals move at more than 1/3-half the speed of the observer for line
transects; were the point transects performed over a "long" time period (ie
not a snapshot))

- were distances measured accurately?

- does the detection function have a wide shoulder?

- is the sample size of observations reasonable? (60-80 recommended,
although for wide shoulders and line transects can get away with far fewer).
If the detection function is estimated by stratum, you'd like 60-80
observations by stratum if possible.

- does the analysis look like it was performed competently?

- do the reported results give both the estimate and CI/CV, and
interpretation of the results take account of the uncertainty in the
estimate.

I've probably forgotten something, but hope this helps.  Perhaps someone
else will be willing to stick their neck out and offer more absolute rules
of thumb!

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: estimating variance of change in density over time
messages.subject_clean: estimating variance of change in density over time
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gavin, list,

If you pool the detection function across years, then comparing the density
estimates is the same as comparing the encounter rates, so you don't need to
worry about 3.109.  You will need the var(n)s or var(n/L)s by year though.
Distance gives you n/L and %CV(n/L) on the Estiamtion Summary - Encounter
rates page of results.  From this you can work out var(n/L) as
(n/L*CV(n/L))^2.  Since in your case the effort varies by year, you're better
working with the n/Ls than the n's for making your comparison.

Were you going to do pairwise t-tests between all pairs of years to look for
changes (yikes!), or just adjacent years, or do some kind of trend analysis?
If the latter, see Chapter 5 of the ADS book.  Simplest would be a linear
regression; if the var(n/L) between years are very different you could weight
by 1/var.

If you think there is some chance that detection probability did vary by year,
but that you don't have enough observations to fit a separate detection
function to each year of data, you could try fitting year as a factor
covariate using the MCDS engine (, or even a non-factor covariate to look for
a linear change in detectability over time -- or you could go further and have
a field for year^2, etc etc).

Hope this helps,

 - Len

Clearly, a few people did not read my previous post regarding how to
unsubscribe.  To curtail the spate of people trying to unsubscribe by posting
directly to the list I have taken the following steps:

1. I have arraged to have a footer added to all messages, describing how to
unsubscribe from the list (see the bottom of this message for an example).
Thanks to Koustubh Sharma for the suggestion.

2. I have temporarily changed the list settings so that all postings have to
be approved by me before they are forwarded to the list.  I don't want to have
to moderate the list in the long term, so will remove this setting in a week
or so if there are no more inappropriate postings.

This is the first time we have had such a breach of "netiquette" in the 6
years that the list has been running, and I hope the last time for another
long while.  Cheers,

 - Len

messages.subject: Estimating SE for pooled density estimates
messages.subject_clean: Estimating SE for pooled density estimates
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I have line transect data for kangaroos in the Victorian mallee country.
Where observations allow data is filtered  and analysed on a stratum by
stratum basis.  However, at some sites with limited numbers of observations
the data is analysed across stratums (mallee and non-mallee) using a global
detection function and post-stratified to estimate density and abundance
within each stratum.

Field staff are interested in total density and abundance estimates and
density and abundance estimates per stratum. This is not the problem.  In
addition they require SE estimates for the pooled density function.  Under
these circumstances Distance provides an output like:

Pooled Estimates:
                         Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence
Interval

------------------------------------------------------
                 DS      2.2521       21.52    15.59  1.4332       3.5389

                 D       5.0254       22.87    19.07  3.1332       8.0603

                 N       934.00       22.87    19.07  582.00       1498.0

Rather than the output below for each strata:

Stratum       : NM
Effort        :    118.9100
# samples     :    11
Width         :    150.1000
Left          :       0.0000000
# observations:    66

    Half-normal key, k(y) = Exp(-y**2/(2*A(1)**2))

                  Point            Standard    Percent Coef.        95%
Percent
  Parameter   Estimate       Error          of Variation     Confidence
Interval
  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------
----------------------
    f(0)     0.15752E-01  0.14796E-02       9.39      0.13065E-01
0.18993E-01
    DS        4.3716      0.95788              21.91               2.7547
6.9378
    E(S)      2.2537      0.17085               7.58               1.9374
2.6216
    D         9.8522       2.2843              23.19               6.0987
15.916
    N         1831.0       424.53              23.19               1133.0
2957.0
  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------
----------------------

Could you please provide me with some advice on how to calculate SE for the
density estimate based on pooled data?  p. 76-77 of Buckland (2001) does
provide equations to estimate variance and confidence intervals, and thus I
could use these to calculate SE, however on the same pages it also states "
we define the coefficient of variation of an estimator to be its standard
error divided by itself".  Thus CV = se / estimate and so se = CV*estimate
or in the above example se (pooled density) = .2287 * 5.0254, = 1.149.

Cameron

messages.subject: Re: question about strip transects
messages.body_plain:
> > As the assumption is that everything is seen within the strip...it

> > seems that the uniform detection function is the only model that
> > fits...g(x) doesn't change over a set distance.  with a 0 adjustment
> > term?

That is correct - on the detection function tab of model definition
properties, select the uniform key function.  Then click on the adjustment
terms tab, click 'manual selection', and set 'Num adj parameters' to zero.

> > the strip width was calculated according to what we could see in the

> > water and pieces of cloth tied to the wings as indicators at a fixed

> > altitude...
> > as D= (average cluster, size)* (encounter rate)/ (2* effective strip

> > width)...then I  set the truncation distance as half the estimate width

> > of the strip....hopefully that makes sense as well.

Yes, that is correct.

I'm glad to see you're planning to try line transect sampling!  I've never
believed that it is plausible that detectability doesn't fall off with
distance from the line.  Typically, you would use a wider strip when using
line transect sampling, and you'll need to give different training to your
observers on how they search.

Steve

messages.subject: Transect Trapping
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am designing a study to look at the density of large fishes in an
expansive wetland adjacent to a canal.  In addition to density, I am
interested in composition as it changes from near canal to central
wetland.  There are several discrete openings in the canal where either
airboats or alligators have created small channels through the sawgrass
that probably serve as corridors for fish movement into the central areas
of the marsh.

I have researched several sampling methods and find that the trapping web
satisfies many of my conditions.  However, within the program WebSim v.2 by
Paul Lukacs is also included an experimental approach called a Trapping
Transect.  Given the potential linear arrangement of fishes occupying
corridors, perhaps a Trapping Transect approach would yield a more accurate
estimate of fish density than a Trapping Web?

I have found no studies referencing Trapping Transects, and the available
documentation on this method is not complete enough to base a study upon.
Is there anyone that can point me to documentation or examples where the
Trapping Transect has been used successfully?

--

messages.subject: Re: Transect Trapping
messages.body_plain:
Mac, list,

Trapping transects are described, and an example given, in Chapter 9 of the
Advanced Distance Sampling book.  If you don't have access to the book via a
local library, you can order a copy at 20% discount via
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.book/advanced.html

Another trapping-based approach, which makes use of recapture information, is
that of Murray Efford.  Links to his papers and the software Density are at
http://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/services/software/density/

Hope this helps,

 - Len

P.S.

> >Given the potential linear arrangement of fishes occupying
> >corridors, perhaps a Trapping Transect approach would yield a more accurate
> >estimate of fish density than a Trapping Web?

I was a bit puzzled by this -- you still have to lay the lines/points down at
random (/stratified random) within your study area (or strata) for valid
inference.  However, other things being equal, trapping lines should have
lower variance than trapping webs in the same way that line transects are in
general more efficient than point transects.

--

messages.subject: Re: cluster size?
messages.body_plain:
This is a difficult problem because it can be viewed as either dependent
detections or underestimating group size.  It is important to recognize
that a group for distance sampling may not be a group from a biological
stand point.  As I view it, a "group" is a collection of animals that
are sighted together.  If as you describe, birds are detected
independently even though they are in close proximity, I would treat
them as separate observations.  Then I would also explore a bootstrap
variance approach to guard against underestimating the variance due to
dependence in detections.

Any other thoughts out there?

--jeff

messages.subject: Re: cluster size?
messages.body_plain:
I am currently utilising Distance sampling on kangaroos, which some of
you may know form very large groups (up to 60 in some instances). I
define a group based on Colin Southwell's work and that is animals that
are detected less than 50m from each other and able to maintain visual
contact. Now these groups may comprise several biological groups (mother
and young-at-foot, sub-adults and dominant males) but they are all
considered one large group because they are all sighted together. I
think it is also important that you keep the definition of the group
consistent throughout the study period.

Hope this helps
Kind regards
Michael

>>> >>> Jeff Laake <jeff....@NOAA.GOV> 21/10/2004 5:05:01 am >>>
This is a difficult problem because it can be viewed as either
dependent
detections or underestimating group size.  It is important to
recognize
that a group for distance sampling may not be a group from a
biological
stand point.  As I view it, a "group" is a collection of animals that
are sighted together.  If as you describe, birds are detected
independently even though they are in close proximity, I would treat
them as separate observations.  Then I would also explore a bootstrap
variance approach to guard against underestimating the variance due to
dependence in detections.

Any other thoughts out there?

--jeff

messages.subject: Line transects and point counts
messages.body_plain:
Good morning all

My name is Martin Taylor and I am an MSc student at the Conservation Ecology
Research Unit at University of Pretoria, South Africa. An initial part of my
research is the evaluation of the bird assemblages of Maputland's
regenerating coastal forests using two distance methods (line transects and
point counts) and subsequently comparing the performance of the two methods.

I have completed an initial field work period with my main field work period
being planned for January/February of 2005. During my initial field work
period I conducted  point counts and line transects in a given habitat to
the point where the curve on a species accumulation curve had flattened
out - for example this would require 6 line transects and 18 point counts in
a certain habitat. A problem I have encountered is that the amount of effort
for a point count (8 mins) is different to that of a line transect (approx
35 mins)making a comparison of community variables obtained from each sample
of each method (such as species richness)  as well as the rate at which the
species accumulation curve flattens out incomparable. I aim to solve this
for the next phase of my field work by walking the transects as per usual
but timing 8 min intervals while walking so as to be able to compare those
"8 min segments" to the 8 mins taken to complete a point count. I would
appreciate it if anybody has any ideas on this approach/ or a better method
as to how to deal with this.

In addition, I plan to sample nests within the coastal dune forests -
initial observations have pointed out that most nests are found following an
observation of bird activity rather than finding the actual nest itself.
Would a strip transect method work better than quadrats?

Thanks alot

Martin Taylor
Conservation Ecology Research Unit

messages.subject: Re: Fwd: [DIST-SAMP] Line transects and point counts
messages.body_plain:
Martin, I don't think breaking recording up into 8 min units is the
solution.  For one thing, you might compromise the line transect design,
ending up with shorter lines in areas of high bird density, and hence
bias.  I think you should design both surveys (line transect and point
transect) optimally, but so that total time in the field is approximately
equal.  You can also adjust your results, to estimate the precision from a
fixed time in the field.  Separately, I'll e-mail you a draft paper that
does just this.  (That paper also argues against point transect counts of
fixed time duration, and in favour of a snapshot approach, because the
former can be biased due to bird movement during the count.)

Note that the term 'point counts' usually refers to just that - counts of
numbers of birds from a point, with no adjustment for detectability.
We tend to use the term 'point transect' when detection distances are
estimated, to distinguish between the two types of survey.

You ask about quadrat counts vs strip transect sampling.  In fact, strict
transect sampling is just a form of quadrat sampling.  The size and shape
of the quadrats depends on what is practical, given size of study area,
whether habitat is open of closed, etc.  You may need to do some
preliminary work to assess what works best.  The danger in your context of
long, narrow quadrats (i.e. strip transects) is that the edge-to-area
ratio is high, so you might end up following quite a few birds whose nests
turn out to be outside the strip.

Steve Buckland
